clue.text: See 3
The wrong side of the tracks at Klosters?

definitions.text: The wrong side of the tracks at Klosters?

parts.words: The wrong side of the tracks at Klosters?
parts.note: at a Swiss ski resort the proper tracks are the groomed runs, so being on the wrong side of them means skiing away from the marked slopes

explanation.surface: A snooty remark about the poor part of a smart Swiss town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The wrong side of the tracks' suggests a poor neighbourhood; at the ski resort of Klosters the tracks are the marked ski runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Skiing away from the prepared runs, in loose unprepared snow, is the sense of this skiing term.

clue.text: Intellectual conformity thus expressed in Mensa link. I'd take right alternative

indicators.note: an alternative arrangement of the letters of these words is called for, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Members of a high-IQ society agree on a link, though one would prefer the right option.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thus expressed in' links the definition to the fodder; 'alternative' rearranges MENSALINKIDTAKERIGHT into the whole saying.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying is used jokingly when two clever people have the same idea, a kind of meeting of intellects.

clue.text: A Sancho Panza with lateral recoil?

parts.note: lateral means to the side
a gun's recoil is its kick

explanation.surface: Don Quixote's squire pictured with a sideways jolt.
explanation.walkthrough: Sancho Panza is Don Quixote's faithful companion, so 'A Sancho Panza' stands for any loyal assistant.
explanation.definitionFit: Sancho Panza is the classic example of a loyal companion who follows a hero about.

clue.text: Withstand this creature!

parts.note: an easel is a stand for a painting

explanation.surface: A command to resist some threatening animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's first word must be split as With + stand.
explanation.definitionFit: The weasel is a small, slender carnivorous mammal, an example of a creature.

clue.text: Just left for a "Patria Mia" rendering

indicators.note: a rendering of the words is a new version of them, so their letters are rearranged
left for a means one letter A is swapped out and an L put in its place

explanation.surface: A performance of a patriotic song described as fair-minded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left for a' swaps one A of PATRIA MIA for L, and 'rendering' then rearranges the result. 'Just' is an adjective meaning fair, not 'only'.
explanation.definitionFit: Just and impartial both describe someone fair who favours no side.

clue.text: Bring six feet up

parts.note: graves are traditionally dug six feet deep, so bringing something up from that depth means digging up a buried body

explanation.surface: An instruction to lift something a short height.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six feet' sounds like a measurement or six people's feet; it is the depth of a grave.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig a buried corpse out of its grave is the meaning of the verb.

clue.text: Mean quality of Pooh's brain? Hardly!

definitions.text: Mean quality of Pooh's brain? Hardly!

parts.words: Mean quality of Pooh's brain? Hardly!
parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh calls himself a bear of very little brain, yet he is never mean-spirited, so the petty trait is hardly his

explanation.surface: Asking whether a cartoon bear's intelligence is stingy.
explanation.walkthrough: Pooh is 'a Bear of Very Little Brain', which literally fits the phrase, but the real sense is pettiness, which he lacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Pettiness of outlook, a mean and narrow attitude, is what this compound noun describes.

clue.text: Reason that hat needed for desert

parts.note: to reason is to infer
tile is old slang for a hat

explanation.surface: Logic says headgear is needed for the arid wastes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desert' is read as an adjective, as in a desert island: barren land.
explanation.definitionFit: Desert land is barren, unable to produce crops, the same sense as unfruitful.

clue.text: Cross to deface, it goes without saying

indicators.note: to is used here in the sense of added to, placing the cross into the middle of the other word

parts.note: to maim is to disfigure or deface
X is the shape of a cross

explanation.surface: Vandalising something with a cross is self-evidently wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it goes without saying' is a jokey definition: a saying that needs no proof.
explanation.definitionFit: A maxim is a saying, a short statement of a truth generally accepted.

clue.text: Corrupt of French, wrapping king in flag

parts.note: de is French for of

indicators.note: wrapping says the flag word goes round the king

parts.note: to flag a path is to pave it with flagstones
R is the abbreviation for king, from Latin rex

explanation.surface: A French monarch wrapped in a banner is accused of corruption.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flag' is a verb here, to lay flagstones, not a banner.
explanation.definitionFit: To corrupt someone morally is to make them wicked or debased.

clue.text: Chekhov's turn, relatively speaking

parts.note: a turn is a stage performance, and among Chekhov's plays this one is about a family tangle of mother, son and lovers

explanation.surface: Chekhov takes his turn to speak, in comparative terms.
explanation.definitionFit: The play by Chekhov about a struggling young writer and his actress mother carries the name of this bird.

clue.text: Time to question the mission

parts.note: to question is to ask

explanation.surface: It is time to cross-examine the purpose of an expedition.
explanation.definitionFit: A mission is an assigned job or duty to be carried out.

clue.text: Economist's crew right to enter the race

parts.note: John Stuart Mill was a famous economist, so his possessive gives the letters

indicators.note: to enter says the right goes inside the crew

parts.note: a crew is a team

explanation.surface: A rowing crew from The Economist enters a boat race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'race' is not a contest but a mill race, the channel feeding a waterwheel.
explanation.definitionFit: A mill race is the current of water that drives a mill wheel, another name for the same channel.

clue.text: British America could be left divided, like our parliament

indicators.note: could be shows the letters of America may become something else, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A political comment that Britain and America might end up as split as Westminster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' is the anagram signal; 'divided' belongs to the definition, since two chambers divide the parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: The UK parliament has two chambers, Commons and Lords, so it is divided into two houses.

clue.text: "I opt to adopt the Establishment with my topper" (Trotsky)

indicators.note: to adopt means to take in, so the Establishment goes inside

parts.note: to opt is to pick, so I opt gives I PICK
CE is the Church of England, the established church

explanation.surface: Trotsky quoted as choosing the Establishment along with his hat.
explanation.walkthrough: Trotsky was killed in Mexico with a blow to the head from this tool, so it 'topped' him: 'topper' is a killer, not a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: To top someone is slang for to kill them; Trotsky's killer used this climbing tool, so it was his topper.

clue.text: Willow-wielding Wizard of Oz

parts.note: cricket bats are made of willow and Oz means Australia, so this is a brilliant Australian batsman

explanation.surface: The Wizard of Oz carrying a stick of willow.
explanation.walkthrough: Oz is slang for Australia; Sir Donald Bradman was the greatest Australian batsman, and a cricket bat is made of willow.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Donald Bradman, the Australian cricketer, had a batting average far beyond anyone else's, a true wizard with the bat.

clue.text: Procuress's tariff uttering bits per second

indicators.note: uttering says the words are spoken, so a word sounding the same is used

parts.note: a bawd is a procuress and her rate is her tariff

explanation.surface: A brothel-keeper's price list read out, with an odd note about data speed.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, BAWD RATE sounds like BAUD RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: The baud rate is the signalling speed of a data line, measured in units per second.

clue.text: Good heavens! He's breathing!

definitions.meaning: an exclamation of surprise or exasperation
literally, a male person still living

explanation.surface: Someone gasps in relief that a man has survived.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a dated cry of astonishment and a literal statement that a man is living.

clue.text: Glorious Revolution's backers back cult. It revolted

indicators.note: revolted means turned over or rebelled, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Supporters of the 1688 revolution are told to support a cult, which then rebelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like a verb meaning support; it is anagram fodder. The Glorious Revolution of 1688 put William III on the English throne; this Whig club upheld it.
explanation.definitionFit: This early 18th-century London club of Whig politicians and writers championed the Protestant settlement of the 1688 Revolution.

clue.text: A good introduction to Rent-a-Poet!

indicators.note: introduction to means putting the letters into the word that follows

parts.note: rent, as a past tense, means tore

explanation.surface: An agency that hires out poets offers a decent first meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' is the past tense of rend, not payment.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabindranath Tagore was a Bengali poet who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1913.

clue.text: Imports a cigar from overthrown president

indicators.note: overthrown says the hidden letters are read backwards
from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A deposed leader brings in a cigar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' takes ORTSAC out of 'Imports a cigar', and 'overthrown' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Fidel Castro was the president of Cuba, famous for his cigars.

clue.text: Child support could be capped

parts.note: a child sits on a lap supported by this joint, and the joint has a cap of bone on its front

explanation.surface: A government limit on child maintenance payments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Child support' and 'capped' suggest welfare payments; the joint a child sits on has a kneecap.
explanation.definitionFit: A small child is bounced on an adult's leg joint, which has a bony cap on its front.

clue.text: A few have sickness benefit

parts.note: five is a few, and V is the Roman numeral five
an ail is an ailment or sickness

explanation.surface: Some people get sickness benefit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sickness benefit' looks like one phrase; the definition is 'benefit' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To be of avail is to be of benefit or use.

clue.text: No stage drunk

parts.note: a leg is a stage of a journey or race
less means without, so it stands for no

explanation.surface: No theatre will host a drunken actor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No stage' reads as no theatre; it is a leg missing. LEGLESS is British slang for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for very drunk, too drunk to stand up.

clue.text: Wild party line detailed in salient structure

parts.note: a rave is a wild party

indicators.note: detailed is read as de-tailed, its last letter cut off

explanation.surface: A rowdy party line is examined in a prominent building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' means 'de-tailed', the last letter dropped. 'salient' is a projecting angle of fortification.
explanation.definitionFit: A ravelin is a V-shaped outwork of a fortress, with its point projecting outward like a salient.

clue.text: Chosen from the pick, or easily discarded

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Someone selected from the best could easily be dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: Chosen (Joseon) is the old name of the country; 'Chosen' looks like a verb meaning selected.
explanation.definitionFit: Chosŏn, or Joseon, was the name of the Korean kingdom until 1910, and is still used in the North.

clue.text: Salvages burst tire during cut back

indicators.note: during says the burst tire sits inside the other word
back means the word for cut is read backwards

parts.note: to cut is to sever

indicators.note: burst says the letters of tire are broken up and reordered

explanation.surface: Someone rescues a punctured tyre during a cutback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tire' is the American spelling of tyre, so 'burst tire' paints a puncture; 'burst' scrambles it to TRIE and 'back' gives REVES, the word for cut turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrieve something is to recover or rescue it, which is what salvaging means.
